newsitem.title: INDIA: Cheap valuations lure foreign funds to India stocks.
newsitem.headline: Cheap valuations lure foreign funds to India stocks.

text.p: Attractive valuations and an improved outlook beyond the short term are drawing foreign funds into bellwether Indian stocks, analysts said on Wednesday.
But investment is being stepped up only in a few sectors fancied for their strong fundamentals, they said.

"Foreign funds are looking at non-cyclicals -- telecoms, power, banks and a few auto firms that cater to the rural markets," Subra Subramanian, Indian research director at securities firm HG Asia, told Reuters.
Analysts said the low price-earnings ratios of Indian stocks, compared to other Asian markets, meant that there was a lot of potential for "good" price appreciations.
"Based on our earnings-per-share growth estimates for 1997, India appears to be one of the least expensive markets in Asia," investment bank Merrill Lynch said in its market strategy.
Merrill forecast that Indian firms would show the highest earnings growth -- 21 percent in 1997 -- compared with other Asian markets like Hong Kong, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand.

"Sectors such as software, banking and pharmaceuticals -- those which are less hit by adverse factors affecting the economy -- are being targeted by foreign funds," said Ajit Verma, a senior analyst at Asian Capital Partners.
India's industrial growth as measured by the index of industrial production (IIP) slowed to 9.8 percent in the April-October period of 1996 against 11.7 percent in the same period a year earlier.
Inflation rose to a 58-week high of 7.75 percent year-on-year in the week ending January 4 this year.
Foreign players remain positive despite the growth slowdown.

"We estimate this year's foreign institutional investment and global depository receipt issues would exceed $6 billion, up from nearly $4.5 billion last year," HG Asia said in its latest India report.
"The current cheap valuations and 19-percent-plus growth projections make us confident about our portfolio flow estimates," HG Asia added.
Market action was focused on benchmark stocks, said Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive at local brokerage Lloyds Securities.

"Frontline stocks such as petrochemical giant Reliance Industries, multinationals Procter & Gamble, Hindustan Lever and Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum, among refinery stocks are the favourites of funds," said a dealer at a foreign firm.
Some analysts say stronger economic growth this year is likely to give the stock market a boost.

"Looking forward into 1997, I expect that rapid economic growth will drive sharp increases in earnings and equity prices," Mark Mobius, director of Templeton Asset Management (India) Pvt Ltd said in a recent letter to investors.
"As valuations are already looking excellent for many stocks on Indian bourses, we will be looking to increase our exposure to the stock market significantly over the next few months," Mobius said.
At 0935 GMT, the Bombay Stock Exchange index was up 2.13 points to 3,504.4.
